title: Inmate death inquest hears about heart stopping in cell
article: The search for what caused the death of a man who was in police custody continued on Tuesday at Prince Albert's Court of Queen's Bench.
The public inquest into Morris Ermine's death is intended to make recommendations to prevent similar deaths in the future.

On Monday, the jury heard from officers who arrested 77-year-old Ermine in July of 2012. He died days after he was found unresponsive in a Prince Albert Police cell and was taken to the Royal University Hospital in Saskatoon.

Ermine was originally going to the detoxification unit, driven by a bylaw officer. However, testimony described him as drunk, irritable, muttering obscenities, and flailing his arms. He was then arrested for intoxication in public and taken to a cell.
On Tuesday, Thomas Thompson a prison guard who was present when Ermine was in a cell, testified.

He described monitoring prisoners every half hour by looking in through their cells. Thompson said he left Ermine in the cell in recovery position on the floor with a blanket because of his level of intoxication.

Later on Thompson saw Ermine on the concrete slab with a blanket around him. Ermine asked for a second blanket, and Thompson told him they usually only give one. Ermine is described as unimpressed by that response but not overly distressed.
Cst. Travis Jordan, who was an acting sergeant at the time, testified Ermine was in his cell for 13 hours.
Jordan received a call from a guard near 4 a.m on July 19, 2012. The guard said Ermine had fallen off his bench for a second time and he may not be breathing.

Jordan said he was at Ermine's cell within a minute, but Ermine didn't respond when talked to or touched. Jordan then called for the staff sergeant, Dave Schluff, and radioed dispatch to call Parkland Ambulance.
Not comfortable enough with CPR to perform it, Jordan said he waited for paramedics to respond as Schluff put Ermine in recovery position.
Ramsay Bellisle responded within minutes.

His testimony detailed a busy night where he was the only one available to respond, and had to take a rover vehicle since all ambulances were out. Although he was alone, Bellisle put a call out for the next available ambulance to come to the police station.
Bellisle noted Ermine was pulseless, breathless, pale, warm and dry in his cell, which meant whatever happened to the man was very recent.
He performed CPR using an automated chest compression device and intubated Ermine. This was to get both his heart beating and oxygen into his lungs.

However, Bellisle testified that a second ambulance arrived quickly after that and had taken Ermine to hospital. During that time his pulse returned. This followed rounds of epinephrine and defibrillation.
Staff Sgt. Schluff joined them so he could operate the chest compression device.
"If it wasn't for those guys [Schluff and Jordan] it wouldn't have gone so well," Bellisle told the court.
Once at the Victoria Hospital, staff took over to stabilize Ermine. Around 6 a.m., Bellisle does remember the call for an ambulance to transfer Ermine to the Royal University Hospital.
The jury also heard from the man who performed the autopsy on Ermine days after he died on July 21, 2012.
Dr. Brent Wilde determined that a case of acute pneumonia, an infection of the lungs, was the most significant factor leading to his death.
This was based on his lungs being heavier than normal lungs because they were filled with fluid and lung inflammation.
Wilde testified that pneumonia can cause poor breathing and oxygen exchange. As a result the heart and brain would have trouble functioning since they rely on oxygen.
Wilde was asked if a heart stopping could be the result of pneumonia, and he explained that the difficulty breathing could present as a cardiac event.
He confirmed that plaque on Ermine's heart and being elderly put him more at risk of catching pneumonia.
Finally, Wilde explained that pneumonia usually develops over several days. This would mean Ermine went into the prison cell with an infection.
The jury noted that in video surveillance shown the previous day, Ermine had not shown the classic symptom of coughing.
Day three of the inquest continues on Wednesday.
